claims.text: Edge cases of the test. (a) For N = 2 and one edge, S = A has a zero diagonal although the graph is connected, so the diagonal of S cannot be required positive and the test looks only at off-diagonal entries. (b) For N >= 3 and G connected the diagonal of S is positive, because every vertex has a neighbour and (A^2)_ii equals the degree of v_i. (c) For N = 1 there are no pairs of different vertices, G is connected, and (I + A)^0 = I = [1] has no zero entry; the sum S is empty, so the test is stated for N >= 2. (d) The pair u = v is always joined by the one-vertex walk of length 0, so 'any two vertices' in Definition 2.1.1 can be read as 'any two different vertices'; the textbook does not discuss u = v (interpretation).

support.quote: The number of walks of length 2 from a vertex to itself is just the number of edges at that vertex, or the vertex degree.

claims.text: Sharpness of the bound N - 1: for the path graph 1-2-...-N with N >= 3, each step of a walk changes the vertex number by exactly 1, so every walk from 1 to N has length at least N - 1; by the walk-counting theorem (A^k)_{1N} = 0 for 1 <= k <= N - 2, so the (1,N) entry of A + ... + A^(N-2) is 0 although the graph is connected. The script confirms the first nonzero power is N - 1 for N = 3, ..., 8, and writes out A, A^2, A^3, A + A^2 and A + A^2 + A^3 for N = 4. Over all labelled graphs with N = 3, 4, 5, 6 the test with N - 2 powers gives a wrong answer on 3, 12, 60, 360 graphs respectively.

claims.text: For every integer m >= N - 1 (N >= 2), the zero pattern of (I + A)^m equals that of (I + A)^(N-1): an off-diagonal entry is positive iff some (A^k)_ij with 1 <= k <= m is positive iff a walk, hence a path of length <= N - 1 <= m, exists; diagonal entries are always positive. Hence G is connected iff (I + A)^m has no zero entry for any one such m, and m = 2^t with 2^t >= N - 1 can be reached by t repeated squarings. Verified by script on all labelled graphs with N <= 6.

claims.text: Cost remark (estimate). With schoolbook multiplication (N^3 scalar multiplications per product of two N x N matrices), reaching A^(N-1) takes N - 2 products: 98,000,000 scalar multiplications for N = 100; repeated squaring of I + A needs ceil(log2(N - 1)) squarings: 7 squarings and 7,000,000 multiplications for N = 100. Breadth-first search with adjacency lists is O(n + m) in the source; when the input is the matrix A it reads each row once, N^2 = 10,000 entries for N = 100. Entries of powers grow fast (largest entry of A^9 for the complete graph on 10 vertices: 38,742,049). Faster matrix multiplication was not examined. Note: claim C39 says 'N - 1 matrix products'; the count is N - 2.

claims.text: The course textbook states no matrix connectivity test and no walk-counting theorem in the pages read (printed pp. 9-12, 21-23, 48-49); Chapters 3 to 8 were not read, so the absence is not established for the whole book.

The two web sources that state the connectivity test prove it loosely. Paramadevan and Sotheeswaran's proof of Theorem 2 applies their Theorem 1 ('different paths') to B = A + ... + A^(n-1), so it counts paths where walks are meant, and its converse passes from a nonzero b_ij to the existence of a path without the walk-to-path lemma. Bai's proof sketch of Theorem 2 likewise says '(I + A)^(n-1) aggregates all paths of length <= n - 1'. Both statements of the test are correct; the proofs are not complete, so the paper proves the test itself (modules/m3.md Section 3.4) and cites the two sources for the statement only.

claims.text: Breadth-first search (BFS) from a start vertex s uses a queue and, in the source, takes the graph as adjacency lists. Its correctness statement: for every vertex v there is a walk from s to v if and only if v is discovered when BFS ends; hence G is connected iff every vertex is discovered from any one start vertex s. (The source's PDF text layer renders the walk arrow as ';'.)
